sections.title: One mass, two directions
teaching: An **oscillation** is repeated motion around an **equilibrium position**, the position where the mass can rest. Moving the mass away from equilibrium makes the spring exert a **restoring force** toward that position. The moving mass continues through equilibrium because of its **inertia**. It then displaces the spring in the other direction, so the restoring force reverses and brings it back again. The return force and the mass's tendency to keep moving together produce the repeated motion.

In **longitudinal motion**, the mass moves along the spring. Moving away from its resting position stretches or compresses the spring. The spring's restoring force opposes that displacement, so stretching and compression are followed by motion back toward equilibrium.

In **transverse motion**, the mass moves across the spring line. The outer ends stay fixed while the middle moves above and below its resting line. The segments are already under tension. When the mass moves off the line, their pulls have components that bring it back toward the line. The restoring action therefore works across the original spring line even though the segments pull along their own directions.

The two examples have the same **frequency**, meaning that they complete the same number of cycles in a given time. Their masses and total effective restoring stiffness are matched, even though their directions of movement differ. Direction alone therefore does not determine how fast the oscillation repeats. These ideal examples have no damping, so the oscillations continue rather than gradually dying away.

restoring force and inertia
longitudinal motion

sections.title: Mass and stiffness change the rate
teaching: **Mass** and **restoring stiffness** affect different parts of an oscillation. Mass determines how difficult it is to change the object's motion. Restoring stiffness determines how strongly the system pulls the object back for a given displacement. Keeping one unchanged while changing the other lets their effects on **frequency** be separated.

A **larger mass oscillates more slowly** when restoring stiffness stays the same. The same restoring action has more inertia to overcome, so the mass takes longer to reverse and complete its motion. The larger blocks and circles therefore finish fewer cycles in the same time than their reference systems. Greater mass changes the rate even though the general back-and-forth pattern remains.

A **stiffer system oscillates faster** when mass stays the same. Displacing it produces a stronger return toward equilibrium, which changes the mass's motion more rapidly. The thicker-spring examples therefore complete more cycles in the same time. A stronger restoring action and a larger mass push the frequency in opposite directions.

These relationships apply to both longitudinal and transverse motion when stiffness means the **effective restoring stiffness in the direction of motion**. For the transverse systems, tension and the arrangement of the segments determine how strongly displacement produces a return toward the resting line. Increasing stiffness along a spring is not automatically the same change as increasing its restoring action across that line. Within each comparison, matching mass and effective restoring stiffness gives the two directions matching frequencies.
concepts: mass resists changes in motion
larger mass lowers frequency at unchanged restoring stiffness
larger restoring stiffness raises frequency at unchanged mass

sections.title: Two masses have two normal modes
teaching: Connecting two masses allows their movements to affect one another through the middle connection. With equal masses, equal coupling elements and both outer ends fixed, the system has two **normal modes**. A normal mode is a coordinated pattern in which the masses keep a particular relationship to one another while the pattern oscillates at its own frequency.

In the **first mode**, the masses move together. When one is displaced in one direction, the other is displaced in that same direction, and they reverse together. This is the lower-frequency pattern. In the **second mode**, the masses oppose one another. When one is displaced one way, the other is displaced the other way. Their opposing movement disturbs the middle connection more strongly, adding to the restoring action and producing the higher frequency.

**Superposition** means adding the displacements contributed by the modes at each instant. Both modes can be present in the same pair of masses. Where their contributions point in the same direction, they add to the displacement. Where they point in opposite directions, they partly cancel. The resulting motion changes as the two modes move through their different cycles.

A mixture containing both modes still contains **two frequencies**. Its more complicated appearance does not turn it into a new single normal mode. The same coordinated relationships occur in the longitudinal and transverse versions when their effective couplings are matched. The higher mode is faster, but it is not simply twice the frequency of the lower one.

sections.title: Three masses have three normal modes
teaching: Three equal moving masses connected between fixed ends have **three independent normal modes**. Each mode specifies how all three masses move in relation to one another. Adding a mass gives the system another independent coordinated pattern, rather than merely making the original pattern larger.

In the **lowest-frequency mode**, all three masses move in the same direction together. The middle mass moves farther from equilibrium than the outer two, whose displacements are equal. Moving together therefore describes their direction and timing, without requiring every mass to travel the same distance.

In the **middle-frequency mode**, the outer masses move in opposite directions while the middle mass stays at equilibrium. Their effects on the middle mass balance in this coordinated pattern. A part of a vibrating system can therefore remain still while other parts continue to oscillate.

In the **highest-frequency mode**, the two outer masses move together and the middle mass moves against them. The connections between the middle and outer masses are disturbed by this opposition, producing a faster pattern. The three mode frequencies are distinct, but they are not simply the first, second and third whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency.

All three modes can contribute to the same motion through **superposition**. Each mass's displacement is the sum of its contributions from the three patterns. The middle mass is stationary in the pure middle-frequency mode, but it moves when the other modes also contribute. A stationary location belongs to a particular mode, rather than being a permanent property of that physical mass in every possible motion.
concepts: three masses and three independent modes
lowest mode moves all masses together with a larger middle displacement
middle mode has opposing outer masses and a stationary middle mass

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode
teaching: A chain has **one independent normal mode for each moving mass** in the direction being considered. The rows extend from one mass to six masses, with a matching number of modes in each row. A smaller chain has fewer independent ways for its masses to move together, so the empty spaces beside those rows do not represent missing examples.

Within a row, the masses and coupling elements stay the same and both ends stay fixed. The lowest mode has all the masses moving together. Higher modes introduce more **reversals in the spatial pattern**, dividing the chain into regions whose displacements point in opposite directions. Following a single mode over time shows those regions reversing together while retaining their relationship.

More reversals within the same chain are associated with a **higher vibration frequency**. Neighboring parts increasingly oppose one another, engaging the couplings in a stronger restoring pattern. The comparison concerns different coordinated motions of the same physical system, rather than different masses or springs being substituted between columns.

The **number of modes** and the **spacing of their frequencies** are separate properties. Having several independent modes does not require their frequencies to be whole-number multiples of the lowest one. These discrete mass chains generally do not form an integer harmonic series. Their displayed maximum displacements are matched to make the patterns comparable, and the colors distinguish mode numbers rather than individual masses.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics
teaching: A string fixed at both ends must have **zero displacement at both endpoints**. These stationary points are **nodes**. The simplest standing pattern fits one half-wave between them, with the middle moving back and forth while the ends stay still. More complex patterns fit additional half-waves into the same length while still satisfying the two fixed boundaries.

The lowest mode has the **fundamental frequency**. The higher examples are **consecutive harmonics**, so their frequencies are whole-number multiples of that fundamental and include both odd and even multiples. Fitting more half-waves into the same string produces a shorter spatial pattern and a faster oscillation. The animation slows all the motions by the same factor so their different rates can be seen without changing these relationships.

Several modes can be present in **one string at the same time**. The combined shape adds their displacements at each position and instant. It can look much more complicated than any individual mode because contributions reinforce or oppose one another differently along the string and as time passes.

A **spectrum** separates the frequencies present in the motion measured at the marked pickup point. Frequency in hertz increases along the horizontal axis, and amplitude increases up the vertical axis. The five peaks correspond to the five harmonic components of the mixture. Their equal heights come from the chosen modal amplitudes at that particular measurement point. Equal peak heights are a feature of this constructed example, rather than a rule that every vibrating string produces.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes
teaching: A **membrane** can form vibration patterns across a surface rather than only along a string. All four edges of this rectangular membrane stay fixed while its interior moves above and below the resting surface. A mode can divide the surface along either of its two directions, so its shape requires more information than a single count along a line.

The two numbers in a **mode label** count the half-wave regions in the two surface directions. The **(1,1)** pattern has one broad moving region. The **(2,1)** and **(1,2)** patterns each divide the surface into two regions, but along different directions. The **(2,2)** pattern divides it in both directions, and **(3,1)** divides it into three along the first direction. Adjacent regions in these divided patterns move to opposite sides of the resting surface, with stationary divisions between them.

The combined surface adds the five modal motions at each location. A marked **pickup point** identifies where that motion is measured. The spectrum places frequency in hertz along the horizontal axis and relative amplitude along the vertical axis. Its five equal-height peaks show the five components present at that point. The chosen modal amplitudes make those measured peaks equal, and the combined surface uses a smaller vertical display scale so its full motion fits in the panel.

The evenly spaced **harmonic frequencies** are deliberately assigned to this illustration. They are not the natural mode frequencies calculated for this rectangular membrane. The example demonstrates how different surface patterns can be combined and represented in a spectrum, while a natural membrane's modes do not automatically form an evenly spaced harmonic series.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction
teaching: A **scientific theory** describes how a system works precisely enough to predict what a measurement should show. **Differential equations** express how quantities change and how those changes depend on the system. Working out the behavior implied by those relationships turns the theory into a prediction that can be compared with the physical world.

The proposed model treats the **vocal folds as a vibrating membrane**. Its stated prediction is that a laryngeal vibration signal will have **equidistant harmonics**, meaning frequency peaks separated by equal intervals. The claim is about an observable pattern in the spectrum, rather than just a resemblance between the appearance of vocal-fold tissue and a membrane.

Testing that prediction would involve measuring **laryngeal vibration**, obtaining its spectrum and examining the spacing between the peaks. Regularly spaced peaks would agree with the stated prediction. A different pattern would raise a question about how well the proposed model describes the measured signal. The comparison links a claim about the physical system to evidence that can be examined.

The supplied material proposes this experiment without reporting a measured outcome. The membrane illustration uses assigned harmonic frequencies, so it does not independently establish that natural membrane modes always have that spacing. The scientific task is to compare the vocal-fold prediction with an actual vibration measurement.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end
teaching: A **fixed end** and a **free end** impose different requirements on a string's vibration. The fixed bottom cannot move, so it is a **displacement node**. The free top can move and forms a **displacement antinode**, where the mode has its greatest displacement. A possible standing pattern has to satisfy both conditions together.

The simplest pattern fits a **quarter-wavelength** between the fixed and free ends. It begins at a stationary point and reaches a moving maximum at the other end. To fit a more complex pattern while preserving those same boundary conditions, the string must gain a full half-wave. That adds another node-to-antinode pair while keeping the bottom stationary and the top at an antinode.

The resulting patterns contain one, three, five and seven quarter-wavelengths. Their frequencies are the **odd harmonics**, consisting of the fundamental and its third, fifth and seventh multiples. An even number of quarter-wavelengths would leave a node at the top, violating the free-end condition. The missing even harmonics therefore follow from what the endpoints allow to move.

The spectrum has frequency in hertz along the horizontal axis and amplitude along the vertical axis. Its four equal-height peaks represent equal excitation of the four illustrated modes when the mixture is measured at the free end. The modes can all contribute there because the free end is an antinode in each pattern. The visible motion is slowed uniformly so the standing shapes and their different rates can be followed.

The fixed–fixed and fixed–free examples are **separately tuned** to share a fundamental frequency. Changing only a fixed endpoint to a free endpoint while keeping the string's length and wave speed unchanged would halve the fundamental. Matching the two examples therefore also requires changing length or wave speed.
